docs.text: Hey! My name is Ash. I'm a third year RAS student.

docs.title: Project Summary
docs.text:
The Smart Gripper we are constructing is an end-effector that uses a five-node architecture. A central Master bus node (powered by a PIC18F57Q43) coordinates telemetry from four dedicated peripheral subsystems: grip actuation, tactile force sensing, infrared proximity detection, and a 3-axis accelerometer utilizing op-amps for real-time slip detection. By continuously polling sensor data and evaluating logic states across the UART network, the master controller dynamically adjusts motor actuation. This closed-loop feedback allows the system to autonomously adjust its grip strength, ensuring it can safely secure delicate items without crushing them and automatically recover if payload slippage is detected.

  • Our team's website can be found here.
  • The Hardware BOM for this subsystem can be found here

docs.title: My Contribution
docs.text: Board 5 - Accelerometer Slip Detection

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Sensor: An ADXL335BCPZ will be used to capture 3-axis accelerometer captures motion and vibration data. The three signals are then ran through high-pass filters and peak detectors by using TLV9062 op-amps before entering the micro controller's ADC (RA0, RA6, RA5).

Power Source: Power is provided through a regulated 3.3V line for the accelerometer and a 5V supply from the PIC18F57Q43 Curiosity Nano powers the signal conditioning array.

Team Connections: Connector 1 will run to our main hub (Sakiya: Board 1) which will then communicate the accelerometer slip detection data to the other boards to adjust the grip accordingly. Pins 1-4 provide digital feedback to the main control board.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Sensor: A SparkFun LIS3DH 3-axis accelerometer breakout (with headers) captures motion and vibration data when an object starts to slip. It talks to the PIC18F57Q43 over I2C (RB1 = SCL, RB2 = SDA), and its INT1 pin (RA0) can alert the microcontroller the moment a motion threshold is crossed. The original plan used an analog ADXL335BCPZ with op-amp filters and peak detectors; that design was dropped because the ADXL335BCPZ only comes in a surface-mount package (see below).

Power Source: A 9V battery feeds the barrel jack and an onboard L7805 regulator, which provides 5V for the Curiosity Nano, LEDs, and push button. An LD1117V33 steps the 5V rail down to 3.3V for the accelerometer breakout and its I2C bus.

Team Connections: The 2x4 interboard connector (J2) runs to our main hub (Sakiya: Board 1). Pin 1 receives UART data from the hub, Pin 2 sends UART data to the hub, Pin 3 carries the shared ESTOP signal, Pin 4 sends the SLIP_INT alert, and Pin 5 is ground.

docs.title: 3-Axis Accelerometer (Slip Detection Subsystem)
docs.text:
1. Analog Devices ADXL335BCPZ 3-Axis Analog Accelerometer

    • $8.88/each
    • DigiKey Product Page
    Pros Cons Small size fits directly on the PCB without needing a separate daughterboard Very small pins make it harder to solder by hand Outputs analog signals for X, Y, and Z axes to go straight into the filters Needs extra capacitors on the board to set the filter frequency Good sensitivity for picking up small slip vibrations and in stock on DigiKey Only runs on 3.3V, so it needs a voltage regulator

  2. NXP MMA7361LCR1 3-Axis Analog Accelerometer

    • $(no info)/each
    • DigiKey Product Page
    Pros Cons Can switch between two sensitivity modes Discontinued part with no pricing or stock available on DigiKey Outputs analog signals that work with the filter design Pads are hidden underneath the chip, making it hard to check solder joints Uses very little power while running Can max out too easily if the gripper moves fast

  3. ROHM KXTC9-2050-FR 3-Axis Analog Accelerometer

    • $19.54/each
    • WinSource Electronics Product Page
    Pros Cons Direct X, Y, and Z analog outputs that work with the filter stages Most expensive option at $19.54 and only available through a third-party broker (WinSource) Uses very low power (240 uA) Tiny 3mm x 3mm package is very difficult to place and solder Filter bandwidth can be adjusted with external capacitors More signal noise at lower vibration speeds and requires a 3.3V line

  4. Analog Devices ADXL345BCCZ 3-Axis Digital Accelerometer

    • $8.01/each
    • DigiKey Product Page
    Pros Cons Least expensive in-stock accelerometer on DigiKey ($8.01) Outputs digital signals, so it will not work with the analog high-pass filters and peak detectors Has built-in tap and motion detection Requires writing extra code to read data over SPI or I2C Mounts directly to the PCB with fewer extra parts Hidden pads underneath the package are hard to inspect after soldering

  5. SparkFun SEN-20659 Triple Axis Accelerometer Breakout - LIS3DH (with Headers)

    • $7.70/each
    • DigiKey Product Page
    Pros Cons Comes with 0.1" through-hole headers, so it plugs into female sockets on the PCB with no surface-mount soldering Breakout board takes up more PCB space and height than a bare chip Digital I2C output removes the need for the high-pass filters, peak detectors, and op-amps Requires writing I2C code to configure the sensor and read data Built-in motion and free-fall interrupts (INT1) can flag a slip immediately; has its own I2C pull-ups and decoupling Limited DigiKey stock (22 at time of ordering) and must run on 3.3V (1.71V - 3.6V)

Original Choice: Option 1: Analog Devices ADXL335BCPZ

Original Rationale: The original design needed an analog accelerometer that mounts directly onto the PCB and sends X, Y, and Z signals into the high-pass filters and peak detectors. Unlike the MMA7361L (which is discontinued with no pricing) and the KXTC9-2050 (which costs $19.54 from a third-party broker), the ADXL335BCPZ is reasonably priced ($8.88) and directly available on DigiKey. It also picks up small vibrations well without maxing out when the gripper moves, and is easier to check for bad solder joints.

Final Choice: Option 5: SparkFun SEN-20659 LIS3DH Breakout (with Headers)

Rationale for the Change: After the schematic review, the ADXL335BCPZ could not be used on this board. It only comes in a 4 mm x 4 mm surface-mount LFCSP package, and this PCB has to use through-hole parts. None of the other analog options solve this, since they are also small surface-mount packages. With instructor approval, an accelerometer breakout board was used instead. The SparkFun LIS3DH breakout (with headers) was chosen because its 0.1" through-hole pins plug directly into two 1x6 female headers on the PCB, it runs off the existing 3.3V regulator, and it costs less than the ADXL335BCPZ ($7.70 vs. $8.88). Because it outputs digital data over I2C, the op-amp high-pass filters and peak detectors were removed from the design, which cut the parts count and cost.

docs.title: 3.3V Voltage Regulator (Power Supply Subsystem)
docs.text:
1. STMicroelectronics LD1117V33 3.3V Linear Regulator

    • $1.27/each
    • DigiKey Product Page
    Pros Cons Outputs a steady 3.3V and provides way more current (800 mA) than the accelerometer needs Most expensive regulator option ($1.27 each) and uses up to 10 mA just to stay on Can step 5V down to 3.3V without any issues Takes up more space on the PCB than smaller regulators Large through-hole package is easy to solder and has built-in overheat protection

  2. Microchip MCP1700-3302E/TO 3.3V Linear Regulator

    • $0.50/each
    • DigiKey Product Page
    Pros Cons Least expensive regulator option ($0.50 each) and wastes almost no power Will burn out if connected to anything over 6V Small through-hole size saves space on the board Only supplies up to 250 mA and cannot handle as much heat Works with standard 1 uF ceramic capacitors

  3. STMicroelectronics LM317T Adjustable Regulator

    • $1.13/each
    • DigiKey Product Page
    Pros Cons Can handle high current (1.5A) and wide input voltages Needs at least 5.3V input to make 3.3V, so it will not work properly off the 5V line Rugged through-hole package Almost as expensive as the LD1117V33 ($1.13) plus needs two extra resistors to set the voltage

Choice: Option 1: STMicroelectronics LD1117V33

Rationale: Since the accelerometer needs 3.3V and the board's main rail is 5V (from the onboard L7805 regulator), a regulator is needed that can drop 5V down to 3.3V. The LD1117V33 does this reliably without needing extra resistors like the LM317T, and its rugged TO-220 package is much harder to accidentally damage during testing than the smaller MCP1700.

docs.title: External Power Source (Power Supply Subsystem)
docs.text:
1. CUI Inc SWI12-9-N-P5 Regulated Wall Supply (via Main Hub / Curiosity Nano 5V Line)

    • $17.71/each
    • DigiKey Product Page
    Pros Cons Gives steady power (up to 1300 mA) without dying during testing Highest upfront cost ($17.71) out of the power options Easily powers the Curiosity Nano, accelerometer, and 3.3V regulator Keeps the gripper plugged into a wall outlet and is not portable

  2. Tenergy 9V 600mAh Rechargeable Li-Ion Battery (30003)

    • $11.99/each
    • DigiKey Product Page
    Pros Cons Allows testing the board without wall cords and costs less than the wall adapter ($11.99) Needs an extra 5V regulator before going into the board Can be recharged instead of buying new batteries Needs a separate battery charger

  3. Energizer EN22 9V Alkaline Battery

    • $2.75/each
    • DigiKey Product Page
    Pros Cons Lowest upfront cost ($2.75) and easy to swap in for quick testing Runs out after about 4.8 hours of use and cannot be recharged Small and easy to clip onto a test board Needs a 5V regulator and turns extra voltage into heat

Choice: Option 3: 9V Alkaline Battery through the barrel jack

Rationale: Having all five team boards plugged into wall outlets at the same time would be difficult to manage, so each board runs from its own 9V battery through a barrel jack. The onboard L7805 regulator turns the 9V into a steady 5V for the Curiosity Nano, LEDs, and push button, and the LD1117V33 then supplies 3.3V to the accelerometer breakout. The battery is inexpensive, easy to swap, and keeps the gripper portable.

MCU Pin Mode Direction Connected To Description RB1 I2C SCL Output LIS3DH Breakout (SCL), J3 Pin 5 I2C clock to the accelerometer (3.3V bus) RB2 I2C SDA Bidirectional LIS3DH Breakout (SDA), J3 Pin 6 I2C data to/from the accelerometer (3.3V bus) RA0 Digital I/O (interrupt-on-change) Input LIS3DH Breakout (INT1) Motion/slip interrupt from the accelerometer RA1 Digital I/O Output J2 Pin 4 (SLIP_INT) Slip alert to Main Hub (Board 1) RA2 UART TX Output J2 Pin 2 (UART_TX) Serial data to Main Hub (Board 1) RC4 UART RX Input J2 Pin 1 (UART_RX) Serial data from Main Hub (Board 1) RB0 Digital I/O (interrupt) Input J2 Pin 3 (ESTOP) Shared emergency stop from Main Hub RA4 Digital I/O Input Push button SW1 (10k pull-up) Test slip alert / clear alert (reads low when pressed) RD0 Digital I/O Output Green debug LED (D3) Status indicator RD1 Digital I/O Output Red debug LED (D4) Slip / fault indicator RA3, RA7, RB3, RB5, RC0, RC1, RC2, RC3, RC5, RD3, RD4, RD5 Digital I/O Unused J3 Extra Header (EH1-EH12) Spare GPIO for debugging and expansion

To meet the requirements of creating this PCB Node, I selected a SparkFun LIS3DH accelerometer breakout, an LD1117V33 3.3V regulator, and a 9V alkaline battery with a barrel jack connector. The ADXL335BCPZ was originally chosen because it was the most reasonably priced and readily available analog accelerometer, but it only comes in a surface-mount package, which the through-hole PCB cannot use. With instructor approval, it was replaced by the SparkFun LIS3DH breakout, which plugs into female headers on the PCB and sends its data digitally over I2C. This removed the need for op-amp filters and peak detectors. While a wall adapter is an option, having all five of our team members' boards plugged into the wall at the same time would be difficult to manage. Instead, a 9V battery with a barrel jack connector feeds into the onboard L7805 regulator to provide a steady 5V for the system while allowing mobility. From this 5V rail, a dedicated LD1117V33 voltage regulator steps the power down to safely supply 3.3V to the accelerometer breakout.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
This Bill of Materials covers every component on my slip-detection subsystem schematic: the LIS3DH accelerometer breakout (I2C), power regulation, debug LEDs and push button, test points, and the Curiosity Nano interface headers. Parts are grouped by supplier:

  • DigiKey: parts being ordered. Quantities follow the class rule of one for the breadboard, one for the PCB, and 1-2 spares, rounded up to a price break where that was cheaper.
  • TECH 162: parts taken from the lab inventory (not ordered).
  • On hand: parts I already own (not ordered).

All parts are through-hole. The accelerometer is a SparkFun LIS3DH breakout with 0.1 in headers (approved by the instructor), which plugs directly into the PCB. The Curiosity Nano board is not included because it is supplied separately.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
This schematic supports a 3-axis accelerometer subsystem built around a SparkFun LIS3DH breakout board, which plugs into two 1x6 female headers and communicates with the microcontroller over I2C. The power management section regulates a 9V barrel jack input down to 5V and 3.3V using L7805 and LD1117V33 regulators, with the 3.3V rail powering the accelerometer. System logic and data handling are managed by a PIC18F57Q43 microcontroller on a Curiosity Nano board, which connects to the main hub (Board 1) through a 2x4 interboard connector carrying UART, ESTOP, and the slip alert signal. The board also includes a 2x8 extra header for spare GPIO, debug LEDs, a push button, and test points on key signals.

Figure 1: Board 5 of Team 104's smart gripper.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: The power budget for the Slip Detection Subsystem was created to verify that the power supply and regulators can support the chosen components in the circuit. It ensures that the L7805 5V and LD1117V33 3.3V regulators can safely power the Curiosity Nano, SparkFun LIS3DH accelerometer breakout, LEDs, and push button without exceeding their maximum ratings. The budget includes a 25% safety margin on each rail and accounts for the idle (quiescent) current drawn by both regulators.

docs.title: Conclusions
docs.text: The system safely operates within its limits. The total current draw on the 9V battery is 124.59 mA, leaving 375.41 mA of headroom. The 3.3V rail requires only 2.50 mA, leaving 797.50 mA available on the LD1117V33. The 5V rail requires 116.59 mA, leaving 883.41 mA available on the L7805. The estimated worst-case battery life of the 9V battery is 4.01 hours, assuming the microcontroller draws its full 50 mA and both debug LEDs are always on.
